Correct, though Kent was in fact convicted. A nolo plea is designed to resolve a criminal charge without an admission usable elsewhere. Rule 410(a)(2) bars it in later civil cases.
Rule 410(a)(3) covers state proceedings, and Rule 410(a)(2) applies to any nolo plea.
questions.e: Rule 410(a) bars, against the defendant, withdrawn guilty pleas, nolo pleas, statements in plea proceedings about them, and statements in failed plea discussions with a prosecutor, in civil and criminal cases alike.

questions.tag: Rule 411: redact the insurance, keep the admission
questions.q:
Immediately after his car hit a cyclist, Pete Sharp told her, "Don't worry, my insurance will cover everything. I wasn't watching the road." In her negligence suit, the cyclist offers the whole statement. Sharp objects to all of it under Rule 411.

What is the best ruling?
o: Admit the entire statement, because it is Sharp's own statement.
Exclude the entire statement, because it mentions liability insurance.
Admit the entire statement, because Rule 411 applies only to insurance policies, not to statements.
Exclude the entire statement under Rule 409, because it promises to pay for her injuries.
Admit "I wasn't watching the road," but exclude the reference to insurance if it can be severed.
oe: The hearsay objection fails as to all of it, but Rule 411 is a separate objection to the insurance reference.
Rule 411 bars only insurance evidence offered to prove negligence. It doesn't sweep away an admission of fault in the same sentence.
Rule 411 covers "evidence that a person was or was not insured against liability," in any form.
Saying insurance will cover it isn't an offer to pay medical expenses, and Rule 409 wouldn't reach the admission of fault anyway.

Correct, though the cyclist would rather the jury hear it all. The admission of fault comes in under Rule 801(d)(2)(A). The insurance reference would invite a decision on an improper basis, so it is redacted where it can be severed without distorting the meaning.
questions.e: Rule 411 bars insurance evidence offered to prove negligence. When insurance is mentioned alongside an admission, the usual result is to admit the admission and redact the insurance reference.

questions.tag: Rule 404(b) reaches later acts
questions.q:
Mara Quinn is charged with knowingly filing a false Medicare claim in March for a wheelchair that was never delivered. She claims the March claim was a billing clerk's mistake. The prosecution offers evidence that in July, four months later, Quinn personally submitted six more claims for equipment never delivered, after an auditor had warned her about the March claim.

What is the best ruling?
o: Exclude it, because Rule 404(b) permits only evidence of prior acts.
Admit it to show absence of mistake and intent, because Rule 404(b) applies to other acts whether they come before or after the charged act.
Exclude it, because acts after the charged offense can't show her state of mind at an earlier time.
Admit it to show Quinn's propensity to commit fraud.
Exclude it, because the July claims are uncharged.
oe: The rule says "any other crime, wrong, or act," without a time limit. "Prior acts" is a common but inaccurate shorthand.

Correct, though later acts feel less probative of an earlier mental state. Repeating the conduct after a specific warning makes an innocent billing mistake in March less likely, a non-propensity chain. The July acts are subject to Huddleston, Rule 403, and a limiting instruction.
Later acts can be probative of earlier intent, especially when the explanation offered is accident or mistake. Timing goes to weight under Rule 403.
Propensity is the barred inference.
No charge or conviction is required (Huddleston).
questions.e: Rule 404(b) covers "any other crime, wrong, or act," including later acts. They may show intent, knowledge, or absence of mistake through a non-character chain, subject to Huddleston and Rule 403.

questions.tag: Rule 404(b): preparation and plan
questions.q:
Two masked men robbed a credit union and escaped in a gray minivan, which was found abandoned an hour later. Leo Grant is charged with the robbery. The prosecution offers evidence that two days before the robbery, Grant stole that same minivan from a mall parking lot, where cameras recorded him. Grant objects that the car theft is an uncharged crime offered to show he is a thief.

What is the best basis for the ruling?
o: Admit it to show preparation and plan, and through them identity, because stealing the getaway vehicle was a step toward the robbery.
Exclude it, because car theft and bank robbery are different crimes.
Exclude it, because Rule 404(b) bars evidence of uncharged crimes.
Admit it to show Grant's character for theft, because both crimes involve stealing.
Admit it only to show motive.
oe: Correct, even though it proves Grant committed a second crime. Stealing the minivan later used in the robbery was preparation for it, part of one overall plan rather than a mere pattern (contrast Kirsch). That links Grant to the robbery without any inference about his character, subject to Rule 403.
Similarity of crimes matters for signature identity, not here. The link is that the minivan was used in this robbery.
Rule 404(b)(2) permits uncharged acts for non-character purposes (Huddleston).
That is propensity reasoning, which Rule 404(b)(1) bars.
Motive is a weak fit. Stealing a car doesn't explain why he would rob a bank. Preparation and plan describe the link.
questions.e: Acts that are steps toward the charged crime, such as obtaining the vehicle, weapon, or tools, show preparation and plan under Rule 404(b)(2). They can identify the defendant without propensity reasoning.

questions.tag: Rule 405(b): entrapment makes predisposition an element
questions.q:
Charged with selling heroin to an undercover agent, Cole Ramsey claims entrapment, arguing the agent badgered him for weeks. The prosecution offers testimony from two witnesses that Ramsey sold them heroin the year before, and a third witness's opinion that Ramsey is a drug dealer.

What is the most accurate statement?
o: All of it is inadmissible character evidence under Rule 404(a)(1).
Only the opinion testimony is admissible, because character must be proved by reputation or opinion.
The prior sales are admissible only to show knowledge, with a limiting instruction.
All of it is admissible, because by claiming entrapment Ramsey made his predisposition, a character trait, an essential element, which may be proved by specific instances as well as opinion.
None of it is admissible unless Ramsey testifies.
oe: Rule 404(a)(1) bars character to prove conduct on a particular occasion. Here predisposition is itself an element of the defense.
That would be right under Rule 405(a). But Rule 405(b) allows specific instances when character is an essential element of a charge, claim, or defense.
Knowledge is a possible purpose, but the stronger and more direct ground is predisposition under Rule 405(b), which permits the propensity use.

Correct, though it means the jury hears that he dealt drugs before. Entrapment puts the defendant's predisposition directly in issue. Under Rule 405(b), when character is an essential element, it may be proved by specific instances as well as reputation or opinion. Rule 403 still applies.
The defense raised the issue by claiming entrapment, whether or not Ramsey testifies.
questions.e: Rule 405(b): when character is an essential element of a charge, claim, or defense (entrapment predisposition, defamation truth, negligent entrustment, custody), it may be proved by specific instances. Self-defense isn't such a case.

questions.tag: Guardia: Rule 403 still limits Rule 413
questions.q:
A physical therapist is charged with sexually assaulting two patients during treatment, and he claims his touching was medically appropriate. The prosecution offers testimony from five other former patients who describe touching during therapy that they considered improper. Experts for both sides disagree about whether each technique described was medically legitimate. The trial court excludes the five patients under Rule 403, finding that the trial would become seven mini-trials on medical propriety.

How will an appellate court most likely rule?
o: Affirm, because Rule 413 doesn't displace Rule 403, and the court reasonably found the risk of confusion substantially outweighed the probative value.
Reverse, because Rule 413 evidence is admissible as of right.
Reverse, because Rule 413 requires courts to presume that propensity evidence is not unfairly prejudicial.
Reverse, because the evidence was also admissible as common-plan evidence under Rule 404(b).
Affirm, because Rule 413 applies only to prior convictions.
oe: Correct, though Rule 413 was enacted to let such evidence in. United States v. Guardia affirmed on nearly these facts. Rule 413 does not displace Rule 403, which applies with its normal balance, and disputes over medical propriety would confuse the jury.
Rule 413(a) says "may admit," and Rule 403 still applies.
Guardia rejected a "presumption in favor of admission" but also held courts may not treat propensity as inherently too prejudicial. The balance is ordinary.
Whatever rule admits the evidence, Rule 403 applies, and the confusion problem is the same.
No conviction is required.
questions.e: Rules 413–415 admit propensity evidence in sex cases but remain subject to ordinary Rule 403 balancing (Guardia). Mini-trials and confusion can justify exclusion, reviewed for abuse of discretion.

questions.tag: Rule 608(b): ask about the act, not the arrest
questions.q:
In a contract suit, the defense wants to cross-examine the plaintiff's key witness about the fact that two years ago she was arrested for insurance fraud, for falsely reporting her car stolen. The charges were dropped. Defense counsel has the police report and an insurance investigator's file showing the car was found in her cousin's garage.

Which question may the court permit?
o: "You were arrested for insurance fraud two years ago, weren't you?"
"You falsely reported your car stolen to your insurer two years ago, didn't you?"
Both questions, because the witness may be asked about any arrest.
Neither question, because the charges were dropped.
Neither question, unless the defense first calls the insurance investigator to prove the act.
oe: An arrest isn't conduct of the witness. It is the police's suspicion, and it isn't probative of her character for truthfulness. Rule 609 requires a conviction.

Correct. Rule 608(b) allows inquiry on cross into specific instances of the witness's own conduct that are probative of untruthfulness, with a good-faith basis (Whitmore). The defense has one in the police and insurance files. Making a false report is the act, and the arrest is irrelevant to it.
Arrests aren't proper Rule 608(b) subjects for this purpose. (Arrests may be asked about on cross of a Rule 405(a) character witness, which is a different situation.)
Dropped charges don't bar inquiry into the underlying conduct, which a conviction isn't needed to show.
Rule 608(b) bars extrinsic evidence. Counsel may ask with a good-faith basis but must take the answer.
questions.e: Under Rule 608(b), cross may ask about the witness's own acts that are probative of untruthfulness, with a good-faith basis and no extrinsic proof. An arrest or charge isn't the act, and only convictions come in under Rule 609.

questions.tag: Rule 609(a)(2): deception element, no balancing
questions.q:
Lana Pierce is on trial for assault and testifies that the victim attacked her. The prosecution offers to impeach her with her conviction three years ago for "theft by deception," a misdemeanor whose elements require obtaining property by creating a false impression. Pierce argues that the conviction is so prejudicial it should be excluded, and that theft isn't usually a crime of dishonesty.

What is the best ruling?
o: Exclude it, because theft offenses are not crimen falsi.
Exclude it, because a misdemeanor can't impeach a criminal defendant.
Admit it only if its probative value outweighs its prejudicial effect to Pierce.
Admit it, because its elements required proof of deception, so Rule 609(a)(2) requires admission with no balancing.
Admit it, but only if Pierce first denies it.
oe: Usually true for simple theft, which is why this is tempting. But this offense's elements require deception, which is what Rule 609(a)(2) asks about.
Rule 609(a)(2) applies "for any crime regardless of the punishment."
That is Rule 609(a)(1)(B)'s balance for felonies. Crimen falsi bypasses it.

Correct, though it is prejudicial and unrelated to assault. Under Rule 609(a)(2), the court looks to the elements (2006 ACN). Because establishing them required proving a dishonest act or false statement, the conviction "must be admitted." Rule 403 doesn't apply.
Convictions are proved by the record or the witness's admission. They aren't limited to cases where the witness denies them.
questions.e: Rule 609(a)(2) requires admission, with no Rule 403 balancing, of any conviction whose elements required proof of a dishonest act or false statement. The label "theft" doesn't control; the elements do. Rule 609(b) still applies to convictions more than 10 years old.

questions.tag: Impeachment by contradiction: "I've never been in trouble"
questions.q:
Before trial, the court ruled under Rule 609(a)(1)(B) that the prosecution could not use defendant Sam Hyde's seven-year-old felony drug conviction to impeach him. On direct examination, Hyde volunteers: "I've never been in trouble with the law in my life. I'd never do something like this." The prosecutor asks to cross-examine Hyde about the drug conviction.

What is the best ruling?
o: Deny the request, because the court already excluded the conviction under Rule 609.
Deny the request, because a defendant's statements on direct can't open the door to excluded evidence.
Allow it, because Hyde's broad denial opened the door to contradiction and to the prosecution's rebuttal of his good character.
Allow it, but only through extrinsic proof of the conviction.
Deny the request, because only crimen falsi may be used against a testifying defendant.
oe: The ruling barred using the conviction to show character for truthfulness under Rule 609. It doesn't license a false impression on a point Hyde chose to raise.
A defendant who makes a sweeping false claim on direct invites contradiction.

Correct, though it undoes his pretrial victory. Saying he's "never been in trouble" is both a false factual claim the prosecution may contradict and an assertion of law-abiding character. Under Rule 404(a)(2)(A), that lets the prosecution rebut, and Rule 405(a) permits inquiry into specific instances on cross. The court still applies Rule 403 and gives a limiting instruction.
Cross-examination is the natural route. The point is that the door is open, not that extrinsic proof is required.
Felonies may impeach a testifying defendant under Rule 609(a)(1)(B), and here the door was opened anyway.
questions.e: A defendant who makes broad claims of a clean record or good character opens the door to contradiction and to rebuttal of character (Rules 404(a)(2)(A), 405(a)), even if the conviction was excluded under Rule 609. Rule 403 and a limiting instruction remain.

questions.tag: Rule 412 applies only where sexual misconduct is alleged
questions.q:
Paul Vance is charged with burglarizing the home of Mia Holt, who identified him from a lineup. He wants to cross-examine Holt about her secret affair with Vance's business rival. He argues she identified Vance falsely to help her lover's business by putting Vance in prison. The prosecution objects under Rule 412, arguing that evidence of a victim's sexual behavior is barred.

What is the best ruling?
o: Exclude it, because Rule 412 bars evidence of any victim's sexual behavior.
Exclude it unless Vance files a motion 14 days before trial and the court holds an in camera hearing.
Admit it only if excluding it would violate Vance's constitutional rights.
Exclude it as a collateral matter.
Rule 412 doesn't apply, because a burglary case isn't a proceeding involving alleged sexual misconduct. The evidence is offered to show bias and is governed by Rules 401–403.
oe: Rule 412(a) applies only "in a civil or criminal proceeding involving alleged sexual misconduct."
Rule 412(c)'s procedure applies only when Rule 412 does.
The constitutional exception in Rule 412(b)(1)(C) isn't needed because the rule doesn't apply. (Olden would support admission even if it did.)
Bias is never collateral (Abel).

Correct, though the evidence is about a sexual relationship. Rule 412 is limited to proceedings involving alleged sexual misconduct. Here the affair is offered to show Holt's motive to lie, which is bias. Bias is admissible subject to Rule 403, and Rule 611(a) protects her from harassment.
questions.e: Rule 412 applies only in proceedings involving alleged sexual misconduct. In other cases, a witness's relationships may be explored to show bias, subject to Rules 403 and 611(a).

questions.tag: Effect on the listener, and the limit on that use
questions.q:
At a drug trial, Officer Grey testifies that he stopped the defendant's car because the dispatcher radioed, "Be on the lookout for a red Camaro, plate ending 42, driver is carrying cocaine for the Southside crew." The prosecution offers the dispatch to explain why Grey stopped the car. In closing, the prosecutor plans to argue that the dispatch shows the defendant was a Southside courier.

What is the best ruling?
o: Admit the dispatch for all purposes, because it explains the investigation.
Exclude the dispatch entirely, because it is hearsay.
Admit the dispatch for all purposes as a present sense impression of the dispatcher.
Admit a limited version, such as that Grey received information about a red Camaro, to explain the stop, but don't allow the accusation about cocaine or the argument that the defendant was a courier.
Admit the dispatch, because the defendant can cross-examine Officer Grey.
oe: Explaining the investigation is a non-truth use. But the prosecutor's planned argument uses it for its truth, which is hearsay (and testimonial).
For the limited purpose of explaining why Grey acted, the dispatch isn't hearsay. The problem is scope, not admissibility of any reference.
The dispatcher was relaying information, not describing an event she perceived.

Correct, though the prosecution wants more. Words offered for their effect on the listener aren't hearsay. But the accusation's only real value is its truth. Rule 403 and Rule 105 call for admitting no more than the background needed and barring use for the truth. That use would also raise a confrontation problem.
Cross of Grey can't test the dispatcher's or the informant's knowledge.
questions.e: A statement offered to explain a listener's conduct isn't hearsay, but the court should admit only what that purpose requires and bar argument from its truth (Rules 105 and 403). Accusatory background can become hearsay, and testimonial, if used for its truth.

questions.tag: Rule 805: two spontaneous layers
questions.q:
A 911 operator testifies that a caller, breathing hard, said: "My neighbor just ran over here screaming, 'Ray shot Tom in the garage! He's still got the gun!'" Neither the caller nor the neighbor testifies at the civil wrongful-death trial. The defense objects to the recording as double hearsay.

What is the most accurate analysis?
o: It is admissible, because 911 calls are business records of the emergency service.
It is admissible if each layer fits an exception: the neighbor's shout as an excited utterance and the caller's report as a present sense impression or excited utterance.
It is inadmissible, because multiple hearsay is never admissible.
It is admissible, because the caller had personal knowledge of what the neighbor said.
It is inadmissible, because the neighbor is unidentified.
oe: The recording might be a record, but the caller and neighbor had no business duty. Their statements need their own exceptions (Johnson v. Lutz; Rule 805).

Correct. Rule 805 admits hearsay within hearsay if each part fits an exception. The neighbor screamed about a shooting while under its stress (Rule 803(2)). The caller described what she was perceiving, the neighbor's arrival and words, while or immediately after perceiving it (Rule 803(1)), and while excited. This is a civil case, so there is no Confrontation Clause issue.
Rule 805 permits multiple hearsay when each layer is covered.
The caller's personal knowledge covers only what the neighbor said. That neighbor's statement still needs its own exception for its truth.
Identity isn't required if the circumstances show perception.
questions.e: Rule 805: split multi-level hearsay and fit each layer to an exception. A caller's description of what she is hearing now can be a present sense impression, and the inner statement needs its own route.

questions.tag: Rule 801(d)(2)(E) in a civil case
questions.q:
Grove Hospital sues two medical-equipment suppliers under state antitrust law, alleging they secretly agreed to fix prices on hospital beds. No one has been criminally charged. Grove offers an email from a sales manager at Supplier A to a sales manager at Supplier B, sent during the alleged agreement: "Hold the line at $9,800 per bed this quarter—Supplier B's boss is on board." Grove offers it against Supplier B. Other evidence shows matching price increases and secret meetings.

What is the best ruling?
o: Exclude it, because the coconspirator exclusion applies only in criminal conspiracy prosecutions.
Admit it against Supplier B as a statement of a coconspirator during and in furtherance of the conspiracy.
Exclude it, because the declarant works for Supplier A, not Supplier B.
Admit it only against Supplier A, as its employee's statement.
Exclude it, because no conspiracy has been proved by a criminal conviction.
oe: Rule 801(d)(2)(E) applies in civil and criminal cases. No conspiracy charge is required, and a joint venture suffices.

Correct, though Supplier B had no control over another company's employee. If the judge finds by a preponderance under Rule 104(a), using the email plus the independent evidence of meetings and pricing, that the two suppliers conspired and the email furthered it, it is admissible against B (Bourjaily).
Rule 801(d)(2)(E) is about coconspirators, not employees.
It is also admissible against Supplier A under Rule 801(d)(2)(D), but Rule 801(d)(2)(E) reaches Supplier B too.
The foundation is a preponderance finding by the judge, not a conviction.
questions.e: Rule 801(d)(2)(E) applies in civil cases. A statement by a coconspirator during and in furtherance of a conspiracy or joint venture is admissible against each member, once the judge finds the foundation under Rule 104(a) with some independent evidence.

questions.tag: Rule 801(d)(1)(C): a composite sketch
questions.q:
Right after a carjacking, the victim worked with a police sketch artist to produce a composite drawing of the carjacker. At trial, the victim testifies and is cross-examined, but she can't identify the defendant in the courtroom. The prosecution offers the sketch, which closely resembles the defendant, and the artist's testimony about how it was made.

What is the best basis for admitting the sketch?
o: As a statement of identification under Rule 801(d)(1)(C), because the victim testifies and is subject to cross, and the sketch identifies a person she perceived earlier.
As not hearsay, because a drawing isn't a statement.
As a recorded recollection under Rule 803(5).
As a public record of the police investigation.
It is inadmissible, because the victim couldn't identify the defendant at trial.
oe: Correct, though she failed to identify the defendant in court. A composite produced from the victim's description is her assertion of what the carjacker looked like, a statement of identification. Rule 801(d)(1)(C) doesn't require an in-court identification. Owens holds that memory problems don't defeat it.
A drawing made to communicate what the perpetrator looked like is an intended assertion under Rule 801(a).
Rule 803(5) requires the witness to vouch for the record, and it is read rather than received. Rule 801(d)(1)(C) is the cleaner, substantive route.
A sketch drawn from a witness's description isn't a matter the officer observed or a factual finding, and Rule 803(8) limits apply in criminal cases anyway.
The exclusion exists precisely for earlier identifications, which are often more reliable than courtroom ones.
questions.e: Rule 801(d)(1)(C) admits a testifying witness's earlier identification of a person, including through a lineup pick, photo array, or composite sketch, even if she can't identify the defendant at trial (Owens).

questions.tag: Post-arrest, pre-Miranda silence
questions.q:
Police arrested Nico Ray at the scene of a stabbing and drove him to the station. No Miranda warnings were given during the ride, and Ray said nothing. At trial, Ray testifies for the first time that the victim pulled the knife on him. On cross, the prosecutor asks, "When the officers arrested you and drove you to the station, you didn't say a word about the victim attacking you, did you?" Ray objects under Doyle.

What is the most likely ruling?
o: Sustain the objection, because using any post-arrest silence violates due process.
Sustain the objection, because the Fifth Amendment bars any reference to a defendant's silence.
Overrule the objection, because Doyle forbids impeachment only with silence after Miranda warnings. Silence after arrest but before warnings may be used to impeach.
Overrule the objection, because Ray's silence was an adoptive admission.
Sustain the objection, because the prosecution may comment on silence only in its case-in-chief.
oe: Doyle rests on the implicit promise in Miranda warnings. Without warnings, there is no such promise.
Impeaching a testifying defendant with silence before warnings is permitted (Jenkins; the Fletcher case).

Correct, though it feels like penalizing an arrested person's silence. The outline notes that pre-arrest and pre-Miranda silence may impeach (the Fletcher case). Doyle protects only silence after warnings, because the warnings implicitly promise that silence carries no penalty.
The question is offered to impeach Ray's trial story, not as an admission adopting an accusation. No one accused him.
Using post-arrest silence substantively in the case-in-chief raises more serious problems than impeachment.
questions.e: Doyle bars impeaching a defendant with silence after Miranda warnings. Pre-arrest silence (Jenkins) and post-arrest silence before warnings (the Fletcher case) may be used to impeach a defendant who testifies.

questions.tag: Rule 804(b)(2): not a homicide case
questions.q:
Bleeding heavily from gunshot wounds, Tom Hale told a paramedic, "I'm dying. Jeff Long shot me over the money." Hale survived but suffered brain damage and now can't remember anything about the shooting. Long is prosecuted in federal court for attempted murder. The prosecution offers Hale's statement as a dying declaration.

What is the best ruling on that ground?
o: Admit it, because Hale believed his death was imminent and spoke about its cause.
Exclude it as a dying declaration, because a dying declaration is admissible in a criminal case only in a homicide prosecution.
Exclude it, because the declarant must actually die.
Exclude it, because Hale isn't unavailable.
Admit it, because dying declarations are admissible in every case.
oe: Hale's belief and subject meet those elements. But Rule 804(b)(2) is limited to "a prosecution for homicide or ... a civil case."

Correct, though every other element is satisfied: he is unavailable through memory loss (Rule 804(a)(3)), believed death imminent, and spoke about its cause. Attempted murder isn't homicide. The prosecution should look elsewhere, for example Rule 803(2), given the stress of the moment.
The declarant need not die, only be unavailable. Hale's memory loss suffices.
Testifying to not remembering the subject matter makes him unavailable under Rule 804(a)(3).
The rule's case-type limit is explicit.
questions.e: Rule 804(b)(2) requires (1) a homicide prosecution or civil case, (2) unavailability (death isn't required), (3) belief in imminent death, and (4) a statement about its cause or circumstances.

questions.tag: Rule 804(b)(3)(B): corroboration binds the prosecution too
questions.q:
At a federal robbery trial, the prosecution offers the statement of an accomplice, now dead, who told his girlfriend, "Me and Dex hit the pawnshop Tuesday. I drove." The statement is offered against Dex. The defense argues that a statement against penal interest offered in a criminal case needs corroboration. The prosecution responds that corroboration is required only when the defendant offers a statement to exculpate himself.

Who is right?
o: The prosecution, because the corroboration requirement protects against defendants fabricating third-party confessions.
The prosecution, because a statement to a girlfriend is nontestimonial and so reliable.
The defense, because Rule 804(b)(3)(B) requires corroborating circumstances clearly indicating trustworthiness for any penal-interest statement offered in a criminal case.
Neither, because Rule 804(b)(3) never requires corroboration.
The defense, because statements implicating others are never against interest.
oe: That was the original concern and the pre-2010 text, which makes it tempting. Since 2010, the requirement applies to statements offered by either side.
Whether a statement is testimonial is a confrontation question. The hearsay exception has its own corroboration requirement.

Correct. The rule now requires corroboration whenever the statement "is offered in a criminal case as one that tends to expose the declarant to criminal liability," whoever offers it. Since 2024, the court considers the totality of circumstances and any evidence that supports or undermines it. The words naming Dex must also be self-inculpatory under Williamson. A statement to a girlfriend sharing blame, "me and Dex," can be.
Rule 804(b)(3)(B) requires corroboration in criminal cases.

Under Williamson, a statement that inculpates others can also be against the declarant's interest, depending on context. A private admission of joint participation to a girlfriend isn't blame-shifting.
questions.e: Rule 804(b)(3)(B): in a criminal case, any statement against penal interest, offered by either side, needs corroborating circumstances clearly indicating trustworthiness, judged on the totality and on evidence for and against it (2024). Williamson limits it to the self-inculpatory parts.

questions.tag: Rule 803(6)(E): the opponent must show untrustworthiness
questions.q:
In a slip-and-fall suit, Valley Market offers its floor-inspection logs, which show an employee initialed "aisle clear" every 30 minutes, including 10 minutes before the fall. A store manager testifies that the logs are kept every day as a regular practice. The plaintiff argues the logs are self-serving and that the store hasn't shown they are trustworthy. She offers no evidence that the entries were falsified.

What is the best ruling?
o: Exclude the logs, because records favoring the party that made them are inherently untrustworthy.
Exclude the logs, because records made in anticipation of slip-and-fall litigation are like Palmer v. Hoffman's accident report.
Exclude the logs unless the store proves they are trustworthy.
Admit the logs, because a business's regularly kept records are admissible unless the opponent shows the source or circumstances indicate a lack of trustworthiness, which the plaintiff hasn't done.
Admit the logs only if the employee who initialed them testifies.
oe: A record's being favorable to its maker doesn't make it untrustworthy. Regular business practice is the guarantee.
Palmer concerned a one-time report prepared after an accident for litigation. Routine logs kept every day for safety are part of regular operations, though the plaintiff may argue the point.
Since 2014, Rule 803(6)(E) puts the burden on the opponent.

Correct, though the store's own logs are self-serving. The manager lays the Rule 803(6)(A)–(D) foundation, and the plaintiff offers nothing beyond suspicion. She can still attack the logs' weight with evidence or on cross.
A custodian or other qualified witness may lay the foundation.
questions.e: Rule 803(6): once the foundation is laid by a qualified witness or certification, the record comes in unless the opponent shows that the source or circumstances indicate a lack of trustworthiness. Routine records differ from one-off litigation reports (Palmer).

questions.tag: Rule 803(8)(A)(iii): the defendant may use it against the government
questions.q:
At his federal bribery trial, the defendant, a city official, offers a report by the city's inspector general. After a formal investigation, the inspector general concluded that the payments at issue were "legitimate consulting fees with no evidence of any improper influence." The government objects that investigative findings are inadmissible in a criminal case.

What is the best ruling?
o: Exclude it, because Rule 803(8) bars investigative findings in criminal cases.
Exclude it, because the inspector general's conclusions are opinions, not facts.
Exclude it, because admitting it would violate the government's right to confront the inspector general.
Admit it, because Rule 803(8)(A)(iii) allows factual findings from a legally authorized investigation against the government in a criminal case, unless the government shows untrustworthiness.
Admit it only if the inspector general testifies.
oe: The limit is one-sided: findings may be used "in a civil case or against the government in a criminal case."
Beech Aircraft held that "factual findings" include opinions and conclusions based on a factual investigation.
The Confrontation Clause protects only the accused.

Correct, though it seems lopsided that the government can't use such findings against the defendant. Rule 803(8)(A)(iii) is deliberately asymmetrical. The government may try to show untrustworthiness under Rule 803(8)(B).
Rule 803 exceptions apply regardless of availability.
questions.e: Rule 803(8)(A)(iii): factual findings (including conclusions, under Beech Aircraft) from legally authorized investigations are admissible in civil cases and against the government in criminal cases, but not against the accused.

questions.tag: Mattox: former testimony at a retrial
questions.q:
At Dale Hart's first murder trial, eyewitness Ivy Lane testified for the prosecution and was thoroughly cross-examined by Hart's lawyer. The conviction was reversed on appeal for an instructional error. Before the retrial, Lane died. The prosecution offers the transcript of her testimony. Hart objects that the jury at his new trial will never see Lane tested by cross-examination.

What is the best ruling?
o: Admit it, because Lane is unavailable and Hart had a prior opportunity, with a similar motive, to cross-examine her on the same charge.
Exclude it, because the Confrontation Clause guarantees cross-examination before the jury that decides the case.
Exclude it, because the first trial was reversed, which voids its record.
Admit it only if the prosecution shows Lane's testimony was reliable.
Exclude it, because prior trial testimony is testimonial.
oe: Correct, though the new jury can't watch her face cross-examination. Mattox v. United States allowed exactly this, and Crawford built on it: testimonial statements are admissible when the declarant is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine. Rule 804(b)(1) also admits the testimony on the hearsay side.
Mattox held that the Clause gives way to "public policy and the necessities of the case" when the witness was cross-examined and has since died.
Reversal for instructional error doesn't erase the testimony or the opportunity to cross-examine.
Crawford rejected reliability as the test. The test is unavailability plus prior opportunity.
It is testimonial, but testimonial statements are admissible with unavailability and a prior opportunity to cross.
questions.e: Under Mattox and Crawford, testimonial former testimony of an unavailable witness is admissible if the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine. Rule 804(b)(1) is the hearsay counterpart.

questions.tag: Rule 106 works against the defendant too
questions.q:
In a sexual-harassment suit, the defendant reads to the jury one line of a text the plaintiff sent a coworker: "Honestly, I thought his jokes were kind of funny at first." The next line of the same text read: "until he cornered me in the supply room and grabbed me." The plaintiff asks the court to require that the second line be read now. The defense objects that the second line is self-serving hearsay.

What is the best ruling?
o: Deny the request, because a party's own out-of-court statements can't be offered on her behalf.
Deny the request now, but let the plaintiff offer the line on redirect if it fits a hearsay exception.

Grant the request, because Rule 106 lets the adverse party require, at that time and over a hearsay objection, introduction of any part that in fairness ought to be considered with the part introduced.
Grant the request, but only for context, with an instruction not to consider it for its truth.
Deny the request, because Rule 106 applies only to recorded statements, not text messages.
oe: Generally true, but Rule 106 overrides the hearsay objection when completion is needed to correct a misimpression the other side created.
Rule 106 entitles the plaintiff to completion "at that time." Waiting would let the misimpression take hold.

Correct, though it lets in the plaintiff's own self-serving words. Reading "his jokes were kind of funny" alone suggests she welcomed his conduct. The next line corrects that. Under the 2023 amendment, completion overrides a hearsay objection. Because the remainder corrects the misimpression only if true, it comes in for its truth.
The ACN says the completing statement comes in for its truth when it corrects the misimpression only if true, as here.
A text is a written statement, and since 2023, Rule 106 covers oral statements too.
questions.e: Rule 106 (2023): when a party introduces part of a statement, the adverse party may require introduction at that time of any other part that in fairness ought to be considered, over a hearsay objection, and for its truth when that is needed to correct the misimpression.

questions.tag: Holmes: bare-suspicion rules remain valid
questions.q:
In a state murder trial, the defendant offers evidence that the victim's business partner had a motive to kill him: the partner stood to collect a $1 million life-insurance payout. The defendant has no evidence placing the partner near the crime or otherwise connecting him to it. The trial court excludes the evidence under a state rule that third-party-guilt evidence must do more than raise a bare suspicion. The defendant claims the exclusion violated Holmes v. South Carolina.

How will a reviewing court most likely rule?
o: Reverse, because Holmes forbids excluding third-party-guilt evidence.
Reverse, because a defendant has an absolute right to present evidence of another's motive.
Reverse, because Chambers requires admitting any evidence favorable to the defense.
Affirm, because states may exclude evidence of third-party guilt that raises only a bare suspicion, judged by the defense evidence's own probative value.
Affirm, because the prosecution's evidence was strong.
oe: Holmes struck a rule that judged the defense evidence by the strength of the prosecution's case, not every limit on such evidence.
The right to present a defense is subject to "established rules of evidence" that aren't arbitrary (Crane).
Chambers involved critical, trustworthy evidence excluded mechanistically. Motive alone isn't critical evidence of guilt.

Correct, though the jury won't hear an alternative suspect. Holmes expressly approved rules excluding third-party evidence that is speculative or remote and raises only a bare suspicion. That rule looks at the defense evidence itself. Motive with no other connection is a classic bare suspicion.
That reasoning is what Holmes condemned. The strength of the prosecution's case is no basis for excluding defense evidence.
questions.e: Holmes distinguishes valid rules excluding third-party-guilt evidence that raises only a bare suspicion, measured by its own probative value, from arbitrary rules that judge it by the strength of the prosecution's case.

questions.tag: Guilbert and Joiner: error, abuse of discretion, harmlessness
questions.q:
At a robbery trial, four eyewitnesses who had known the defendant for years identified him. A fifth, a stranger, identified him after a brief, high-stress encounter at gunpoint. The defense offered an expert to testify about weapon focus, stress, and cross-racial identification. The trial court excluded the expert as describing "common sense." Surveillance video and the defendant's fingerprints on the getaway car also implicate him. He was convicted.

What is the most likely appellate result in a court that follows Guilbert?
o: Reversal, because excluding a qualified eyewitness expert is always reversible error.
Affirmance, because eyewitness experts are never helpful to juries.
Reversal, because the expert would have testified that the stranger's identification was mistaken.
Affirmance, because evidentiary rulings are never reviewable.
The exclusion was an abuse of discretion as to the stranger's identification, but harmless given the strong corroborating evidence.
oe: Even an erroneous exclusion is reviewed for harmlessness.
Guilbert rejected the "common sense" rationale, noting a near-national consensus that such testimony can help.
Under Guilbert, the expert may describe general factors but may not opine on whether a particular eyewitness is accurate.
Rulings admitting or excluding experts are reviewed for abuse of discretion (General Electric Co. v. Joiner).

Correct, though it leaves the conviction standing. State v. Guilbert held that excluding the expert was an abuse of discretion only as to the stranger. Four acquaintance identifications and physical evidence made the error harmless. Review is for abuse of discretion, then harmlessness.
questions.e: Under Guilbert, eyewitness-identification experts are admissible when helpful. They may explain general factors but may not opine on a particular eyewitness's accuracy. Exclusion is reviewed for abuse of discretion (Joiner), then harmlessness.

questions.tag: Rule 703: opinion in, inadmissible basis presumptively out
questions.q:
At a civil-commitment hearing before a jury, the state's psychiatrist testifies that the respondent is dangerous. Her opinion rests largely on the respondent's mother's report that he punched her last month. Psychiatrists routinely rely on such family reports. The mother won't testify, and her report is inadmissible hearsay. On direct, the state asks the psychiatrist to tell the jury exactly what the mother said.

What is the best ruling?
o: Exclude the opinion, because it rests on inadmissible hearsay.
Allow the opinion and the mother's statement, because the psychiatrist relied on it.

Allow the opinion, but bar the state from disclosing the mother's statement unless its value in helping the jury evaluate the opinion substantially outweighs its prejudicial effect. The respondent may elicit it on cross.
Allow the mother's statement as substantive evidence that he punched her.
Exclude the opinion unless the mother testifies.
oe: Rule 703 lets experts rely on inadmissible facts of a kind experts in the field reasonably rely on.
Reliance permits the opinion but doesn't open the door to disclosure by the proponent.

Correct, though the jury will hear an opinion without its main support. Rule 703's last sentence creates a presumption against disclosure by the proponent of inadmissible bases. Melton explains why: a jury can't use the punch to evaluate the opinion without believing it happened. The opponent may bring the basis out on cross (Rule 705).
Reliance doesn't make hearsay substantive.
The opinion is admissible without her, based on what experts reasonably rely on.
questions.e: Rule 703: an expert may rely on inadmissible facts of a kind reasonably relied on in the field. The proponent may disclose them to the jury only if their probative value in evaluating the opinion substantially outweighs their prejudicial effect (Melton). The opponent may explore them on cross.

questions.tag: Photograph: a witness who didn't take it
questions.q:
In a premises-liability case, the plaintiff offers a photograph of a broken stair tread. The photographer is unknown. The building's maintenance supervisor, who inspected the stairs the morning after the fall, testifies that the photo fairly and accurately shows the stairs as he saw them that morning. The defense objects that no one can say who took the photo, when, or with what camera.

What is the best ruling?
o: Exclude it, because only the photographer can authenticate a photograph.
Admit it, because a witness with knowledge testifies that it fairly and accurately depicts the scene as he saw it.
Exclude it, because the "silent witness" foundation requires evidence of the camera's reliability.
Admit it, because photographs are self-authenticating.
Exclude it under the best evidence rule unless the negative is produced.
oe: Under the pictorial-testimony approach, any witness who saw the scene can authenticate the photo.

Correct. The defense's points sound substantial, but under the "pictorial testimony" theory (Rule 901(b)(1)), a witness with knowledge who testifies that the image fairly and accurately shows what he saw is enough. Who took it doesn't matter. Timing questions go to weight.
The silent-witness foundation (Rule 901(b)(9)) is needed when no witness saw what the image shows. Here the supervisor did.
Photographs aren't listed in Rule 902.
The plaintiff isn't proving the content of the photo as such, and a print is an "original" under Rule 1001(d) anyway.
questions.e: Photos and videos are authenticated either by a witness who saw the scene and says the image is fair and accurate ("pictorial testimony") or, without an eyewitness, by showing a reliable process ("silent witness," Rule 901(b)(9); State v. Luke).

questions.tag: Rule 1004(d): a collateral writing
questions.q:
A witness in a car-accident case testifies that she remembers the accident happened on March 3 because she had just picked up that day's newspaper, which had a front-page story about a local election. The defense objects under the best evidence rule that the plaintiff must produce the newspaper to prove what it said.

What is the best ruling?
o: Sustain the objection, because the witness is testifying to the content of a writing.
Sustain the objection unless the plaintiff shows the newspaper was lost without bad faith.
Overrule the objection, because the newspaper is self-authenticating.
Overrule the objection, because newspapers are public records.
Overrule the objection, because the newspaper's content isn't closely related to a controlling issue, so other evidence of it is admissible.
oe: Technically she does describe a writing's content, which is what makes the objection tempting. But Rule 1004(d) excuses the original when its content is collateral.
Loss is one excuse (Rule 1004(a)). Rule 1004(d) is a separate one that needs no showing about the original.
Authentication is separate from the best evidence rule.
A newspaper isn't a public record, and Rule 1005 would require a certified copy anyway.
Correct. The election story only helps the witness fix the date. Under Rule 1004(d), other evidence of content is admissible when the writing "is not closely related to a controlling issue."
questions.e: Rule 1004 excuses the original when (a) it was lost or destroyed without bad faith, (b) it can't be obtained by process, (c) the opponent has it and was on notice, or (d) it is not closely related to a controlling issue.

questions.tag: Fisher and Doe: preexisting documents in the lawyer's hands
questions.q:
Facing an IRS investigation, a business owner gave his lawyer the company's general ledgers and invoices from 2022, prepared in the ordinary course of business, so the lawyer could advise him. The government subpoenas the lawyer for the documents. The owner argues that they are protected by the lawyer-client privilege because he gave them to his lawyer in confidence, and by his Fifth Amendment privilege.

What is the most accurate statement?
o: The documents are privileged, because the client gave them to the lawyer in confidence to obtain legal advice.
The documents are protected by the client's Fifth Amendment privilege wherever they are kept.
The documents are privileged only if they would have been protected in the client's own hands, and preexisting business records generally aren't protected there by the lawyer-client privilege.
The documents are protected, because the subpoena is directed at a lawyer.
The documents are protected, because the lawyer has a duty of confidentiality.
oe: Giving documents to a lawyer in confidence protects them only if they would have been privileged in the client's hands (Fisher). Preexisting records aren't communications.
The client isn't compelled when a subpoena goes to his lawyer, so his Fifth Amendment privilege isn't implicated (Fisher).

Correct, though the owner gave the documents to his lawyer to get advice. Under the Fisher case, the lawyer-client privilege protects communications, not preexisting documents. The Fifth Amendment doesn't protect documents in the lawyer's hands, since the client isn't compelled. Transfer to a lawyer protects them only if they would have been protected in the client's hands. Ordinary business records generally wouldn't be.
Lawyers can be subpoenaed for unprivileged materials.
The ethical duty of confidentiality isn't an evidentiary privilege.
questions.e: Fisher and Doe: (1) the privilege covers communications, not preexisting documents; (2) the client's Fifth Amendment privilege doesn't reach documents held by the lawyer; (3) documents transferred for advice are protected only if they would have been protected in the client's hands; (4) the Fifth protects only compelled testimonial self-incrimination. Rule 501 leaves these questions to federal common law.

questions.tag: Government lawyers: a circuit split
questions.q:
A federal grand jury investigating corruption subpoenas a state governor's former chief counsel to testify about conversations with the governor regarding state contracts. The governor's office asserts the lawyer-client privilege. The prosecutor argues that government officials can't use the privilege to withhold evidence from a federal criminal investigation.

What is the most accurate statement of the law?
o: The privilege never applies to government lawyers, because they serve the public.
The privilege always applies, exactly as it does for private clients.
Every circuit holds the privilege yields to a federal grand jury.
Courts are divided: the Second Circuit upheld the governor's office's privilege against a federal grand jury, while the Seventh, Eighth, and D.C. Circuits have limited it in criminal investigations.
The Supreme Court resolved the issue in Swidler & Berlin.
oe: No court takes this categorical view. Government entities have the privilege in many settings.
Several circuits limit it in federal criminal investigations.
The Second Circuit disagreed in the Rowland grand jury case.

Correct, though it gives no single rule. The Second Circuit (In re Grand Jury Investigation, the Rowland case) refused to abrogate the privilege because the investigation was criminal, acknowledging conflict with the Seventh Circuit and tension with the Eighth and D.C. Circuits (the Lindsey case). The outline treats this as an unsettled syllabus topic.
Swidler & Berlin held that the privilege survives the client's death. It didn't address government lawyers.
questions.e: Government lawyer-client privilege in federal criminal investigations is unsettled. The Second Circuit (Rowland) upheld it, and the Seventh, Eighth, and D.C. Circuits have limited it. Swidler & Berlin concerns survival after death.

questions.tag: Marital confidences: children present, divorce later
questions.q:
While married, Carl and Dana Wren had a conversation at home in which Carl confided that he had been forced by threats to sign over his share of a business. Their two-year-old and infant were in the room. They later divorced. In a civil suit, the business's buyer calls Dana to testify about the conversation. Carl objects. Dana is willing to testify.

What is the best ruling?
o: Dana may testify, because the privilege ended with the divorce.
Dana may testify, because the children's presence destroyed confidentiality.
Dana may testify, because she, as the witness-spouse, decides whether to testify.
Dana may testify, because the conversation concerned financial matters, which aren't privileged.
Carl may prevent the testimony, because the communication was confidential when made during a valid marriage, and the privilege survives divorce.
oe: The marital-confidences privilege survives divorce. (The testimonial privilege, by contrast, needs a valid marriage when claimed.)
Rakes held that the presence of infant children didn't defeat confidentiality.
That is Trammel's rule for the testimonial privilege, which applies only in criminal cases. Under the confidences privilege, either spouse may prevent disclosure.
Rakes rejected a general exception for financial matters.

Correct, though Dana wants to testify. United States v. Rakes, on similar facts, held such conversations privileged: divorce and the presence of very young children didn't matter, and there is no exception for financial matters. The privilege applies in civil cases and either spouse may assert it.
questions.e: Marital-confidences privilege: confidential communications during a valid marriage; either spouse may prevent disclosure; it survives divorce; it applies in civil and criminal cases; young children's presence doesn't defeat it (Rakes). Exceptions cover joint crimes and crimes against family members.

questions.tag: Rule 501: a state privilege for a state-law claim
questions.q:
In a federal diversity suit for defamation under state law, the plaintiff seeks to depose the defendant's father about what his 30-year-old son told him in confidence about the statements at issue. The state where the court sits recognizes a parent-child privilege by statute. Federal common law recognizes none.

What is the best ruling?
o: The father must testify, because federal courts don't recognize a parent-child privilege.
The father must testify, because the son is an adult.
The father may refuse, because under Rule 501 state privilege law governs a claim for which state law supplies the rule of decision in a civil case.
The father may refuse, because Jaffee requires federal courts to recognize privileges adopted by any state.
The father must testify, because the parent-child privilege applies only in criminal cases.
oe: True of federal common law (In re Grand Jury Proceedings), which makes this tempting. But Rule 501's second sentence sends state-law claims in civil cases to state privilege law.
Whether the state's privilege covers adult children depends on the state statute, and the facts say the state recognizes it here.

Correct, though the federal rule rejects any parent-child privilege. Rule 501 provides that "in a civil case, state law governs privilege regarding a claim or defense for which state law supplies the rule of decision." Defamation under state law qualifies.
Jaffee looked to state consensus as "experience" in shaping federal common law. It didn't require adopting every state's privileges.
The scope of the state's privilege is a question of state law. Nothing suggests it is limited to criminal cases.
questions.e: Under Rule 501, federal common law governs privilege, except that in civil cases, state law governs privilege for claims or defenses governed by state law. No federal parent-child privilege exists (In re Grand Jury Proceedings).
